articles.headline: Balanced Montana State attack led by trio of veteran returners | Key matchup
keyFacts: Gonzaga plays Montana State on Tuesday night at McCarthey Athletic Center.
Montana State's attack is led by returning veterans Jeremiah Davis, Christian King, and preseason all-conference point guard Jed Miller.
The game presents a perimeter test for Gonzaga after allowing LSU to make eight second-half three-pointers in a recent loss.
body: Nov. 16—Gonzaga may not be able to pinpoint a single matchup when Montana State rolls into town for Tuesday night's contest at McCarthey Athletic Center.

In many ways, that's part of the vision and strategy for fourth-year coach Matt Logie, who brings back a talented, experienced roster that received seven of the 11 first-place votes in the Big Sky preseason coaches poll and 19 of the 32 first-place votes from media members.

How's this for balance and symmetry? Montana State's top two scorers, guard Jeremiah Davis and forward Christian King, not only average the same scoring number (13.8 points), but they're also in lockstep when it comes to rebounding (4.5) and assists (1.8).

Both are worthy candidates for Tuesday's key matchup, but it would be difficult to exclude point guard Jed Miller, the only returning All-Big Sky First Team performer on Logie's roster and the lone Montana State player to show up on the Preseason All-Conference team.

"I think that's part of the secret sauce to our group is we're not designed around one or two players," said Logie, who coached at Whitworth from 2011-19. "We're a very equal opportunity, free-flowing group that enjoys sharing the basketball. Jeremiah and Christian have both really picked up where they left off last season in terms of their own personal growth and development as both scorers and leaders in our program.
"Obviously Jed Miller is the face most people know as the returning first team all-conference point guard and somebody we have tremendous confidence and experience competing with."

It should be a good test for Gonzaga on the perimeter three days after the Bulldogs consistently left LSU's shooters open, allowing the Tigers to make 8 of 14 from behind the arc in the second half and win the game on Donovan Dent's step-back 3-pointer in the closing seconds.
Davis, King and Miller take 16 combined 3-pointers per game. Davis leads the group in 3-point percentage (46.7), followed by King (38.5) and Miller (35.6).

King, senior from Seattle whose father Rich was selected No. 14 overall by the NBA's Seattle SuperSonics in 1991, spent two seasons at Washington before transferring to Montana State. He led the Bobcats with 18 points in 26 minutes during a 77-52 win over Cal Poly on Sunday.

A native of Compton, Davis was a Big Sky All-Defensive selection for Montana State after becoming a full-time starter as a redshirt junior. He's been the team's leading scorer in three of four games to this point.
Miller has appeared in 106 games for the Bobcats over five seasons. The Aguora Hills, Calif., product averaged 14.9 ppg, 5.7 rpg and 2.9 apg in 2025-26.

Regardless of how the Zags play it, they should have the size advantage at every position in Tuesday's matchup. The 6-2 Miller will likely start on 6-4 Xaivian Lee with 6-7 Davis Fogle handling the 6-4 Davis and 6-10 Braden Huff starting on the 6-8 King.

articles.headline: Asuma, Evans power Minnesota over Western Illinois 99-63
keyFacts: Minnesota defeated Western Illinois 99-63 on Monday, led by Isaac Asuma with 21 points and Kyan Evans with 16 points and 10 assists.
Minnesota built a 54-27 halftime lead after shooting 74.1 percent from the field in the first half.
Minnesota will host Oklahoma State on Friday, and Western Illinois will play UAlbany at home on Friday.
body: MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Isaac Asuma scored 21 points, and Kyan Evans had 16 points and 10 assists as Minnesota rolled past Western Illinois 99-63 on Monday.
The Golden Gophers (5-0) shot 74.1% from the field in the first half, making 20 of 27 shots and 10 of 17 from 3-point range to build a 54-27 lead at the break.

Minnesota opened the game with nine straight points and led 18-6 after Nolan Groves’ layup with 13:16 left. The Gophers continued pulling away behind Asuma and Evans, who combined for seven first-half 3-pointers.
Evans hit a 3-pointer with 1:38 remaining, and Nolen Anderson followed with another from beyond the arc before Malick Kordel’s dunk sent Minnesota into halftime with a 27-point advantage.
Asuma finished 8 of 11 from the field and added seven assists. Jaylen Crocker-Johnson had 11 points and nine rebounds, while Kordel scored 12 off the bench.
Minnesota shot 67% overall, made 15 3-pointers and finished with 32 assists on 39 field goals.
Jack Riley led Western Illinois (1-4) with 14 points. Daivion Traylor added 10.
Up next
Minnesota: Hosts Oklahoma State on Friday.
Western Illinois: Plays UAlbany at home this Friday.

body: Monday night's matchup between the Grizzlies and Wizards was billed as a clash of soon-to-be titans in the NBA landscape.
Cameron Boozer and AJ Dybantsa jostled for draft position during the 2025-26 college season. Dybantsa won the proverbial battle, hearing his name called first during June's draft.
Boozer has responded with a vengeance in the duo's nascent professional careers, spearheading Memphis ascent up the Western Conference table with steady displays on both ends of the floor.
Facing against a lowly Washington bunch that entered the game having lost its last seven, Boozer affirmed that his recent outings were no aberration.

Boozer canned seven triples, taking advantage of a porous Washington defense to power Memphis' offense. He added seven rebounds and seven assists, flaunting his multifaceted skillset as the Grizzlies charted a path back into the contest.
The 19-year-old made history with his latest display, becoming the youngest player to record at least 25-points, five-rebounds, five-assists and five made three pointers in the same game.

articles.headline: Biden library nears site decision as fundraising trails ambitions: report
keyFacts: Former President Joe Biden's library foundation is closing in on a Delaware location amid early fundraising challenges, CBS News reported.
Donors' willingness to fund the project reflects Biden's standing after frustrations over his presidency and his son's pardon, reports noted.
Jill Biden is expected to assist with fundraising while Joe Biden undergoes prostate cancer treatment, according to the report.
body: Former President Joe Biden’s presidential library foundation is reportedly closing in on a location in Delaware, even as its fundraising efforts continue to fall short of expectations.

Despite receiving several multimillion-dollar gifts in 2026, the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation is working to overcome a difficult fundraising start, following a roughly $600,000 deficit in 2025, according to filings reported by CBS News.

The foundation reportedly raised $1.5 million in 2025 but spent $2.1 million. An official told the outlet that the organization was not actively soliciting donations that year, characterizing it instead as a "building and infrastructure year."

The expenses, which were partly covered by contributions from Biden’s presidential inaugural committee and individual donors, primarily went toward staff, consultants and legal fees. Roughly $250,000 was specifically paid to consultants tasked with laying the groundwork for the foundation’s fundraising operation, the outlet said.
EX-DEM FUNDRAISER TORCHES BIDEN AS BOOK LAUNCH IMPLODES: 'NO ONE WANTS TO READ'
This year, the foundation secured two $5 million gifts among its donations, according to reports.

CBS News noted that the foundation is now seeking to capitalize on the post-midterm political climate, as wealthy Democrats reportedly poured money into campaigns that helped fuel sweeping victories for the party.
Despite this year's fundraising recoveries, some of Biden’s close allies have reportedly criticized Democratic donors for failing to proactively offer support for his library.
Biden has "never been a good fundraiser, even when he was in the Senate," one source said.
His wife Jill is also expected to help with fundraising as Biden undergoes treatment for prostate cancer .
JOE BIDEN SAYS CANCER SLOWED HIM DOWN, LIMITING MEMOIR PROMOTION TOUR

The foundation has also expanded its board with five new members, bringing in a mix of diplomatic, business and nonprofit experience as it seeks to strengthen its fundraising efforts, according to reports.

The reported additions include Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, Biden’s former ambassador to Brazil; Bijan Sabet, a venture capitalist and former ambassador to the Czech Republic; event planner Bryan Rafanelli; Wilmington nonprofit leader Logan Herring; and Annie Tomasini, a former White House deputy chief of staff.
OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.

The library’s fundraising performance could offer a window into Biden’s standing within the Democratic Party and the extent to which wealthy donors are still willing to contribute to preserving his political legacy. His support among some donors has been strained by frustrations with his presidency and his decision to pardon his son, Hunter.

As Biden works to build financial support for the project, the foundation’s fundraising total still pales in comparison with that of President Donald Trump’s presidential library foundation , which has already secured tens of millions of dollars.
Trump’s donor list has been led in part by major media and technology companies that have aligned themselves with the president, including Meta, Elon Musk’s X and Paramount, according to reports.

articles.headline: Ukraine: Russian strikes hit bridges in Kyiv, mayor says
keyFacts: Russian strikes hit two major bridges in Kyiv, damaging infrastructure and disrupting water and heating supplies, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Ukraine struck a bridge in Crimea and targeted Moscow with drones in its largest assault on Russia, officials said.
Ukrainian, European, and US negotiators are discussing future talks with Russia on ending the war.
body: What you need to know
- Russia struck two important bridges in Kyiv, mayor Vitali Klitschko said
- Ukraine on Monday launched its biggest drone attack on Russia, hitting a strategically important bridge in the annexed Crimean peninsula
- The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026:
Ukraine hits the Crimean Bridge for second day in a row, Russian authorities say
Ukraine struck a bridge connecting the annexed Crimean peninsula and the Russian mainland late Monday.
The same bridge over the Kerch Strait was also struck a day earlier, Russian-installed authorities said.
"At the moment, traffic is suspended," Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov said Tuesday.
Russian officials also said Ukraine had struck oil refineries on Monday.
Monday's drone attack was the largest such assault on Russia since it launched itsfull-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Overnight into Tuesday, Ukraine targeted Moscow with nearly 200 drones.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said early Tuesday morning that Russian air defenses had downed 20 drones heading towards the capital.
Russia hits two major bridges in Kyiv: What we know
Russia struck two bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv late Monday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
"According to preliminary information, there have been hits on the North and South bridges in the capital," Klitschko said on Telegram.
In a later post, Klitschko said the attack "caused damage to critical infrastructure," adding that there were "disruptions to water and heating supplies" because of strikes.
Earlier this month and in October, a series of Russian attacks hit several bridges in the Ukrainian capital, causing major disruption.
Earlier on Monday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned Russia was planning strikes for Monday night and into Tuesday.
"Tonight, overnight, and throughout tomorrow, please pay attention to missile danger alerts," he said.
"And they there, in Russia, must know that for every one of their evils there will be our just response," Zelenskyy added.
Welcome to our coverage
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital were struck in an overnight Russian attack.
The strikes damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted water and heating in parts of the city, Klitschko said.
Ukraine on Monday attacked Russia, targeting Moscow with drones and striking an important rail bridge in the annexed Crimean peninsula.
The latest exchanges come as negotiators from Ukraine, Europe and the US discuss future talks with Russia on finding a path to peace.

articles.headline: Iran rules out nuclear site inspections until war ends
keyFacts: A senior Iranian official said Tehran will bar international inspectors from damaged nuclear sites until the war permanently ends.
Vice President JD Vance said the Trump administration will not let the war with Iran become a two-year commitment.
Iraqi troops prepared to enter Jurf al-Sakher after officials set a Friday deadline for an Iran-backed militia to leave.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- A senior Iranian official said Sunday that Tehran will not allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to return to examine damaged nuclear facilities until the war has "permanently ended." IAEA inspectors visited Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant in September but have not gained access to other sites targeted by the U.S. since started.

- Hostilities around the Persian Gulf have also increased in recent days, with attacks on commercial vessels continuing and Iran claiming another attack targeting a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain. Bahraini officials said the weapons were intercepted, and the U.S. military denied a similar claim from Iran late last week.
Vance says there's "no daylight" between him and Trump on war with Iran
In an interview with Fox News that aired Monday night, Vice President JD Vance said "there's no daylight" between himself and President Trump, after he was asked about his being the reason for .
"I think there's no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration," Vance told Laura Ingraham.
Vance also said that neither he nor the president want the conflict to become a forever war.

"... We have accomplished an extraordinary amount. We have destroyed the nuclear program. We have destroyed Iran's conventional military," Vance said. "... The President of the United States has a lot of options, right? He could say, 'We're done now.' He could of course, exert more military and diplomatic pressure on the Iranians. I think it's something he's thinking about doing right now, right? What are we actually going to do to finally bring this thing to a resolution?"

Vance positioned himself as a skeptic of foreign military entanglements before he became vice president, and early in the Iran war, Mr. Trump conceded that Vance was "philosophically, a little bit different than me" and "less enthusiastic about going." Still, Vance has publicly stood by the president on the Iran war, and helped lead a U.S.-Iran diplomatic push over the summer.
Another tanker hits naval mine in Strait of Hormuz, Iranian officials say
A tanker struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday and caught fire, according to Iranian state media.
It is the fourth such incident in 24 hours, the Islamic Republic of Iran Navy told semi-official news agency ISNA in a statement. Officials did not identify the vessel or provide further information.

Meanwhile, a British maritime agency on Monday said it received a third-party report of an attack involving a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz, just north of Khasab, Oman. The incident disabled the vessel and resulted in an engine room fire, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.
"The crew have been reported safe. Damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at the time of this report," the UKMTO said.
Vance says U.S. won't let Iran war become 2-year commitment
Vice President JD Vance told Fox News that the Trump administration won't let the Iran war become a two-year commitment. He also said the Iranian nuclear program was still a threat to the U.S.

"We told the American people we would do no more forever wars. Yes, the president felt he had to destroy the nuclear program, and, yes, the Iranian nuclear program is a threat to the United States of America," Vance told Fox News' Laura Ingraham in a clip from an interview expected to air Monday night. "But we are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment or, frankly, even a two-year commitment."

The U.S. and Israel started the war at the end of February. Throughout the conflict, President Trump has said that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. The Iranian regime has maintained for years that its nuclear program is for peaceful purposes.

"Despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever, we're not going to stay there forever," Vance told Ingraham. "We promised we wouldn't, and I have full confidence the president will get us out of this thing with great results."
U.S. Central Command posts photo of newest carrier in Middle East
U.S. Central Command posted on Monday a photo of the newest aircraft carrier operating in the Middle East, the USS Theodore Roosevelt.

A U.S. military official confirmed to CBS News senior national security correspondent Charlie D'Agata on Sunday that the Roosevelt had joined the two other carriers in the region, the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington.
Central Command said the Roosevelt was in its area of responsibility as part of a scheduled deployment.
The three ships aren't all expected to remain in the area for long as carrier strike groups rotate through the region.
Iran's Houthi allies say 37 people killed or wounded by Saudi strikes in 24 hours
Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said Monday that Saudi attacks had killed or wounded 37 people in the past 24 hours.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said in a post on social media that "the toll of the Saudi aggression during the past 24 hours reached 37 martyrs and wounded," citing the Houthi-run health ministry.
Houthi authorities said earlier that three Yemenis, including a child, were killed in two separate Saudi strikes in areas held by the rebels.
Health ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said a child was killed in a drone strike that hit a house in the al-Sarar quarter of the capital, Sanaa, which also wounded seven others.
Separately, two people were killed and eight more wounded in airstrikes Monday morning on a private fuel station in Harf Sufian district in Omran province, al-Asbahi said.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
Iran reportedly claims Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes endorsed by U.S. are "fully mined"

A Saudi news outlet closely linked to the government and ruling royal family cited Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as claiming Monday that southern shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz, which the Trump administration and U.S. military have insisted are safe and open, have been "fully mined."
There was no immediate statement from the IRGC itself echoing the report by Saudi Arabia's Asharq News, which is not technically state-run, but owned by a state-backed institution in the kingdom.
Iran has made daily claims of commercial ships hitting sea mines in and around the Strait of Hormuz for weeks, some of them corroborated by independent monitors confirming fires on board vessels.
Iran insists the southern lanes, which skirt the Omani coast, are unsafe and that all vessels must use other routes close to Iranian shores.
U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper reiterated the Trump administration's claim at the end of October that "Iran's navy is all at the bottom of the sea."

"We also successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognized primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines," he said, adding that "U.S. forces remain highly vigilant and present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."
Iran's foreign minister meets Pakistan's army chief

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held talks in Islamabad on Monday with Pakistan's army chief, who has served as a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran throughout the war, according to a post on his official Telegram account.

During the meeting with Gen. Asim Munir, "the two sides reviewed regional and international developments" and "exchanged views on existing challenges and threats to regional peace and security," said the statement by Araghchi.
Pakistan, along with Qatar and Turkey, has tried to mediate a peace deal between Iran and the U.S. for months.
Pakistani foreign minister says Mecca pact nations to meet in Islamabad this month

Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar said Monday that senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey - the countries that signed onto the trilateral Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in the summer - would meet in the Pakistani capital later this month.

Pakistan signed the mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey in August. It is, like the much larger NATO alliance co-founded by the U.S. after World War II, a vow to come to each other's defense in the event of an attack on any member.
"The apex committee of this body ... will be actually meeting, hopefully, end of this month, in Islamabad," Dar said.

Saudi Arabia continues to face repeated attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, who have targeted major commercial airports, oil facilities and shipping infrastructure since fighting in Yemen's civil war intensified in July.
Both Turkey and Pakistan have sent troops to Saudi Arabia as part of the mutual defense agreement.
CBS/AFP
2 Houthi drones intercepted over Saudi Arabia, Saudi-led military coalition says
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said it had intercepted two Houthi drones targeting Saudi cities on Monday.
Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said in a brief post on X that the two drones were "intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca and Riyadh regions."
Earlier Monday, Houthi health authorities said three Yemenis, including a child, were killed in two separate Saudi strikes in areas the rebels hold in Yemen.

A group allied with Yemeni government forces said, meanwhile, that its fighters had pulled out of areas along Yemen's coastline near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – the southern gateway to the Red Sea and thus a vital chokepoint for commercial shipping – amid relentless attacks by the Houthis.
Iraq orders army to enter stronghold of Iran-backed militia
Iraqi army forces were ordered Monday to enter a town near Baghdad considered a stronghold of the powerful following accusations of oil smuggling.

Kataib Hezbollah, a U.S.-designated terrorist group that has launched attacks on American forces in the region, has controlled the town of Jurf al-Sakher, about 40 miles south of Baghdad, for 12 years, according to The New Arab. Previous Iranian proxy groups in Iraq such as Kataib Hezbollah.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi "ordered the armed forces to enter" Jurf al-Sakher, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi told state news agency INA, adding that "a deadline has been set for the armed faction to exit the area." A security source told the AFP news agency the deadline was Friday.

Fighting between the army and the Iran-backed militias is possible, sources told The New Arab. A senior Iraqi official said the government had deployed tanks, armored vehicles and troop carriers to the outskirts of Jurf al-Sakher, and that forces were ready to push into the town.
CBS/AFP
Oil prices continue downward trend, U.S. diesel drops below $6 a gallon
The price of oil continued its downward trend Monday morning despite ongoing tension and attacks on commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf amid the unresolved U.S.-Iran war.

Brent crude, the international standard for oil, declined 0.5% to $95.34 per barrel, still much higher than the approximately $72 a barrel in late February before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran. Benchmark U.S. crude fell 0.3%, to $88.31 a barrel.
The International Energy Agency said last week that Gulf exports "recovered much faster than global oil demand."
Consumer prices for gas and diesel have seen a slight decrease in recent weeks, but they remain higher than pre-war levels.
The average price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. fell below $6 Monday for the first time since it crossed that threshold in September.
CBS/AP
Houthi rebels claim 3 killed, including a child, in Saudi airstrike
Houthi health authorities said Monday that three Yemenis, including a child, were killed in two separate Saudi Arabian strikes in areas the Iran-backed rebels hold in Yemen.
Health Ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said a child was killed in a drone strike on a house in the al-Sarar quarter of the capital, Sanaa, which also wounded seven others.
Separate airstrikes Monday morning hit a private fuel station, killing two people and wounding eight in Harf Sufian district in Omran province, al-Asbahi said.
Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia, which made no immediate comment on the strikes.
CBS/AFP
U.S. envoy calls on Iran-backed Hezbollah to disarm
A U.S. envoy on Monday called on Iran-backed Hezbollah to voluntarily give up its weapons - which the Lebanese group has always rejected.

On a visit to Lebanon, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz called on Hezbollah to disarm and hand its weapons over to Lebanese state authorities, saying: "No country can have two armies."
"I think the message should be loud and clear, that Lebanese sovereignty must be fully restored," said Waltz, "and the mechanism to do that will be the Lebanese armed forces."

Fighting between Hezbollah and Israel has eased since the summer, but the conflict remains a hurdle to any final peace deal between the U.S. and Iran. Iran and Hezbollah have demanded the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon and a total halt to fighting in the country as part of any ceasefire agreement between Washington and Tehran.

An agreement signed in June between the Israeli and Lebanese governments to end the fighting in southern Lebanon linked Israel's withdrawal from the country with Hezbollah's disarmament, and Hezbollah has refused to give up its weapons.
CBS/AFP
France expects EU to approve new sanctions against Iran after store fridges hacked

France is asking the European Union to impose new sanctions against Iran after cyberattacks, which the French and later the Belgians , targeted refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Monday he was "confident" that measures targeting those responsible for the hack would be agreed at the next gathering of EU foreign ministers in Brussels in December.

"I have come to Brussels today to present evidence concerning those primarily responsible for this extremely serious cyberattack, and to request that European sanctions be imposed against them within one month," Barrot told reporters. "I am pleased to have secured the support of a vast majority of European Union member states."

On Oct. 11, major grocery store chains in France were that caused "significant food spoilage" and triggered around 20 fires as temperatures in refrigeration units shot up, according to the country's prosecutor's office.

French officials believe Iran was behind those attacks, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying it out. Belgian authorities have drawn the same conclusion about a that hit refrigeration units in stores in several European nations.

Iran has denied responsibility for the cyberattacks, which come after months of warnings from the regime that it could respond to ongoing hostilities by the U.S. and its allies with unspecified asymmetrical warfare - and a that Tehran's are evolving to target civilian infrastructure.
CBS/AFP
Iran claims regional 10-nation bloc backs its proposed 2-day deal
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that a 10-nation regional bloc had backed Tehran's proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under an initial ceasefire with the United States.

Tehran has said it is prepared to reopen the strait within two days if Washington agrees to its . After initially proposing a seven-day implementation period, Iranian negotiators the proposed timeframe to two days, calling it a "sign of good will."
The Trump administration has thus far , which include the U.S. releasing frozen Iranian financial assets, easing sanctions and lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, as "unacceptable."
Araghchi's comments came during a meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organization, a group of nations from Central and South Asia and the Middle East.

"The meeting responded positively and, by supporting the plan proposed by Iran, namely the two-day plan, expressed hope that this plan would lead to a definitive and comprehensive ceasefire," Araghchi told reporters in Islamabad.

Senior officials from Pakistan, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Iran, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan attended the meeting in the Pakistani capital, but there was no immediate confirmation from the other nations attending the meeting that they had backed the Iranian proposal. Afghanistan is also a member of the bloc.
CBS/AFP
Israeli military says it struck a Hezbollah weapons shipment
The Israeli military said Monday that it had struck a Hezbollah weapons shipment along the Syria-Lebanon border.
"The weapons were intended to strengthen Hezbollah's operational capabilities to carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF soldiers," the Israel Defense Forces said in a post on X.
Lebanese state media also reported that Israel had struck a mountainous area in eastern Lebanon.

"Enemy aircraft launched a strike at dawn against the Al-Shaara region, in the highlands of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range, without resulting in victims or damage," Lebanon's official National News Agency (NNA) said.

Large-scale hostilities between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon have eased in recent months, but sporadic fighting continues. The conflict has complicated efforts by the Trump administration to wind down the war it launched jointly with Israel against Iran more than eight months ago, as Tehran insists any ceasefire must include all fronts in the region, including Lebanon and Gaza.
CBS/AFP
Iran, British monitoring agency report tankers hit in and near the Strait of Hormuz
A British naval monitoring agency said Monday morning it had received a report of a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz being struck.
The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center said the vessel was "struck by an unknown projectile whilst transiting outbound," resulting in a fire in the engine room.
It added that crew members were all accounted for and no casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, Iran's state broadcaster said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had caught fire after hitting a naval mine, citing Tehran's navy.
It said the ship was traveling through a "restricted area," which "exposes offending vessels to serious risks."
Iran's armed forces regularly report similar incidents with ships Tehran deems to be transiting the Strait of Hormuz without its permission.
Iran-backed Houthis tighten control of key strait after Yemeni troops pull back
A group allied with the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said its fighters pulled out from areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait amid relentless attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis.

The Southern Armed Forces said they would now focus on securing Yemen's southern city of Aden, held by the internationally recognized government, as well as trying to break the Houthi siege of the crucial city of Taiz.
The move has allowed the rebels to consolidate their grip on the strait, in a setback to the Saudi-backed efforts to dislodge them from the strategic coastal territories on the Red Sea.
Local media reported that the Houthis fired two ballistic missiles on the district of Buraiqeh on Aden's western coast.
Clashes were reported between the Houthis and government forces in an area in Yemen's southwestern province of Lahj, which has key supply routes close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strategic waterway is a key chokepoint for Saudi Arabia's oil exports, and has been the focus of fighting in the region for months.
Houthi rebels have tightened their grip on the strait in recent months, threatening to disrupt the flow of Saudi oil through the Red Sea.
CBS/AP
Iran rules out inspections of damaged nuclear sites until war ends
A senior Iranian official said Tehran would not allow inspections of nuclear sites damaged by the war with the U.S. until the war had "permanently ended."

"We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran's conditions are met and the war has permanently ended," Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised interview late Sunday.
The remarks came after the International Atomic Energy Agency, a nuclear watchdog, urged Tehran to take steps toward resuming inspections, which have been partly suspended since last year.
IAEA inspectors visited Bushehr nuclear power plant in September but have not gained access to other sites targeted by the U.S., including Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan.
Gharibabadi said the agency's request to inspect damaged facilities was "likely aimed at assessing the effectiveness of American weaponry."
CBS/AFP
Army whistleblower alleges senior military officials ignored warnings ahead of deadly attack in Kuwait

A U.S. Army soldier who survived a deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran.

The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday and obtained by CBS News.

He alleges Army leaders dismissed concerns over thin fortifications at a U.S. command post in Kuwait where six American soldiers were killed by an Iranian drone in the first 24 hours of the conflict, the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war.
The complaint also claims the post — known as Port Shuaiba — "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."

"I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself - all the way down to my level," Maj. Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. "We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn."

Ramsbottom spoke with 60 Minutes as part of an eight-month investigation into the March 1 attack at the command post, known as Port Shuaiba. The day after the attack, in a press conference, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well-protected.
Iran claims attack on U.S. assets in Bahrain

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its forces carried out a drone attack on a U.S. radar system at a base in Bahrain, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster on Sunday.

"The U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the IRGC said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.
Bahrain's military later said it had intercepted Iranian airstrikes before they hit their targets.
The interior ministry in an X post urged "residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels for the protection of public safety."

There was no immediate comment from the U.S. military's Central Command about the claim on Sunday. CENTCOM on Friday rejected a similar claim from the IRGC, which said it had attacked a "U.S. early-warning radar" in Bahrain.

articles.headline: The Mississippi tragedy is another wake-up call for America
keyFacts: Two University of Mississippi students died from synthetic substances, according to former DEA acting administrator Derek S. Maltz.
Maltz stated that Chinese chemical suppliers and Mexican cartels traffic dangerous synthetic drugs into America.
Maltz urged a national strategy combining aggressive international enforcement, mandatory school drug education, and expanded treatment resources.
body: The tragic deaths of two University of Mississippi students should serve as another wake-up call for America. Dangerous synthetic substances are increasingly reaching unsuspecting consumers through deceptive marketing, unregulated products, and sophisticated international supply chains run by greedy transnational criminal networks.

What happened is not an isolated tragedy. It is part of a much larger and evolving threat that has been building for years. From synthetic cannabinoids and fentanyl to nitazenes , kratom products of questionable origin, counterfeit pills, and illicit vaping products, criminal organizations continue to exploit America’s vulnerabilities while putting public health and safety at risk.

After 28 years with the Drug Enforcement Administration , including serving as acting administrator and director of the Special Operations Division, I have witnessed firsthand how transnational criminal networks exploit America’s vulnerabilities.

The chemicals change. The packaging changes. The trafficking methods evolve. But the criminal business model remains the same: maximize profits while disregarding the devastating consequences for American families.

For decades, China-based chemical suppliers have played a significant role in the global synthetic drug trade. From precursor chemicals used to manufacture methamphetamine to synthetic cannabinoids such as K2 and Spice, bath salts, and eventually fentanyl, these supply networks have repeatedly adapted to changing laws and enforcement pressure.

Chinese chemical suppliers and Mexican cartels have helped fuel a deadly fentanyl trafficking pipeline. Today, emerging synthetic opioids, including nitazenes, and increasingly concentrated or chemically modified kratom-related products present additional challenges for law enforcement and public health officials.
America is confronting an evolving synthetic drug threat that extends far beyond fentanyl.

One particularly troubling development is the proliferation of unauthorized vaping products and other questionable substances sold through convenience stores, gas stations, smoke shops, and online marketplaces.

Colorful packaging, appealing flavors, and reassuring promotional claims may create the misleading impression that these products are safer than they are. Consumers may have limited knowledge of the chemicals these products contain, their origins, or the potential health risks they present.

In September 2025, federal authorities announced the seizure of approximately 4.7 million unauthorized electronic cigarettes valued at $86.5 million. Almost all the illegal shipments identified during that operation originated in China. Authorities reported deceptive shipping descriptions and inaccurate valuations intended to circumvent import controls.

Unauthorized vaping products, synthetic opioids, and concentrated kratom-related substances are not identical threats, and their risks must be evaluated separately. However, the use of deceptive marketing, questionable supply chains, and illegal distribution practices warrants aggressive investigation.
This is not simply a drug enforcement problem. It is a challenge for public safety, public health, and national security.

International criminal networks increasingly exploit global commerce, digital communications, complex financial systems, and weaknesses in regulatory enforcement. Disrupting individual shipments or arresting street-level distributors is not enough.

We must identify the manufacturers, chemical suppliers, importers, distributors, financial facilitators, and domestic businesses knowingly enabling illegal activity. The United States also needs greater accountability and meaningful cooperation from China in targeting chemical suppliers and criminal financial networks implicated in the illicit drug trade.
But enforcement alone will never solve this crisis.
We must attack both the supply and demand sides of the problem with equal urgency.

Mandatory, age-appropriate drug education in schools should become a national priority. Young Americans need accurate, compelling information about counterfeit pills, dangerous synthetic substances, illicit vaping products, and the growing risks associated with an unpredictable illicit drug supply.
We should also recruit professional athletes, entertainers, celebrities, and influential social media personalities to deliver lifesaving messages on the platforms young people use every day.
At the same time, we must expand access to treatment, recovery services, and evidence-based prevention programs for those struggling with substance use disorders.
For nearly two decades, I have watched dangerous synthetic substances emerge, spread, and evolve faster than our traditional response systems.
We cannot continue playing an endless game of chemical whack-a-mole while American families suffer devastating losses. The illegal chemical imports are often from the same criminal ecosystem.
The deaths at Ole Miss are another painful reminder that these dangers can reach any community, any campus, and any family.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CRACKS DOWN ON CHINA-NVIDIA CHIPS LOOPHOLE

America needs a coordinated national strategy that combines aggressive international enforcement, supply-chain accountability, mandatory education, and meaningful treatment and recovery resources. The safety of our children, our communities, and our nation depend on stopping the flow of illicit substances and illegal products coming from China and other foreign countries before more lives are lost.
We owe it to the families who have lost loved ones and to the next generation to act before another tragedy becomes tomorrow’s headline.

Derek S. Maltz is the former acting administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration. During his 28-year DEA career, he served as director of the Special Operations Division, leading complex international investigations targeting transnational criminal organizations.

articles.headline: Adan Diggs commits to Arizona: Five-star combo guard becomes first member of Wildcats' 2027 recruiting class
keyFacts: Five-star combo guard Adan Diggs committed to Arizona on Monday evening as the first member of the Wildcats' 2027 recruiting class.
Diggs chose Arizona over Arkansas, Kentucky, and USC, according to the report.
247Sports Director of Scouting Adam Finklestein stated that Arizona is getting one of the more naturally gifted two-way prospects in the national class.
body: Five-star combo guard Adan Diggs committed to Arizona on CBS Sports HQ on Monday evening. The No. 6 overall player in the 2027 recruiting cycle by 247Sports marks the first member of the Wildcats' upcoming recruiting class.

The Goodyear, Ariz., product committed to the Wildcats over Arkansas, Kentucky and USC. Diggs is the second-highest-ranked player from the 2027 recruiting cycle to pledge his college commitment. Last month, DeMarcus Henry — the No. 4 overall player in the class — committed to North Carolina.

Other players from the 2027 recruiting class who recently committed include five-star center Lewis Uvwo (Providence), five-star guard Reese Alston (LSU), five-star forward Jordan Page (UConn) and four-star forward Asa Montgomery (Duke).

Diggs is just the latest five-star that coach Tommy Lloyd has landed since arriving at Arizona in 2021, joining Caleb Holt (2026), Koa Peat (2025) and Brayden Burries (2025). 247Sports Director of Scouting Adam Finklestein says that Arizona is getting "one of the more naturally gifted two-way prospects in the national class."

"Physically, he has solid size for a combo-guard, good length (6-foot-7 wingspan), and an emerging power body. He's a good, not great, vertical athlete, who is better when he can elevate off two, and also a fluid mover. He's a very talented defender, both on and off the ball. He has some versatility, but can also impact the game around the rim. He's athletic and competitive on the glass (6.1 per game in EYBL) and capable of being the weakside low-man and even challenging plays at the rim."

Arizona finished with the second-best recruiting class in 2025 and ranked No. 13 last cycle (2026) in the 247Sports rankings. With a commitment from Diggs, Arizona is on track to finish with one of the top classes in the 2027 recruiting cycle.

articles.headline: Buying a used phone? Make sure to check the IMEI first
keyFacts: Checking a pre-owned phone's IMEI number reveals whether the device has a questionable history and what networks it can access.
Every mobile device has a unique 15-digit IMEI number that network providers use for identification and blacklisting stolen phones.
Buyers should verify a seller-provided IMEI on researched lookup websites to confirm the device has not been reported stolen.
body: Buying a used phone? Make sure to check the IMEI first
A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.

Smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many. However, whenever you're buying a refurbished or generally pre-owned phone, you need to take a few precautions. In particular, you need to look out for the red flags of a potential scam and every mobile device has a special number that can help you.

Buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work. You should properly clean and sanitize the secondhand phones you find while also making sure the phone you're getting doesn't have any obvious defects. When you're asking the seller about the device's condition and history, you should also ask about the phone's IMEI number — which can reveal whether a phone has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to, and more.
What IMEI numbers are for and how to find them

Every mobile device has a unique 15-digit number associated with it known as an International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number. This number is used to register your phone with your network provider and can subsequently be used by that provider to identify your phone. If your phone is lost or stolen, you can contact your provider and have them blacklist your phone via that IMEI number.

If you want to find your phone's IMEI number, it can typically be found in the device's packaging or on any physical or digital receipts, as well as on your network provider account. Additionally, while you can generally find your IMEI number in your phone's settings, dialing *#06# into the keypad of any phone will reveal its unique IMEI code. You can also contact your provider's support team about finding this number if all else fails.
Why you should ask sellers for a phone's IMEI number

If you're in the position of buying a new phone, the device's seller should provide its IMEI code to you upon request — and you should definitely ask for this code. The IMEI number will help you confirm whether it's been stolen or whether it's compatible with certain cellular networks.

There are all too many scams to avoid when buying refurbished tech online and in person, so be on the lookout for sellers that refuse to provide the IMEI number as they may be selling fenced goods. An IMEI number can't be used to hack or track phones by itself but sellers should only share it with serious buyers through private messaging and buyers should keep screenshots of the conversation just in case.

Upon being provided with an IMEI number, you should proceed with checking its validity and whether it's been reported stolen or lost. There's quite the smorgasbord of sites to use if you want to check an IMEI number, many of which will ask for a small fee before checking the number. While many of the options are free, research whichever site you use first to make sure you're not about to fall for a phishing scam.

articles.headline: Joe Biden blames son Hunter’s legal woes for disastrous 2024 debate performance vs. Trump
keyFacts: Joe Biden wrote that distress over his son Hunter's felony convictions negatively affected his 2024 debate performance against Donald Trump.
Biden claimed that the federal prosecution against his son was politically motivated by Republicans seeking to hurt him.
In his memoir, Biden also recalled threatening Senator Joe Manchin over a proposed federal pandemic relief package.
body: “In many ways, this debate prep was no different from any other I had undertaken over the years,” Biden wrote. “Except for one thing. I felt awful— so bad I was tested for COVID.”
The 46th president said his test came back negative but “something else was weighing on” him, “beyond the exhaustion.”
“On June 11, my son Hunter had been convicted of three felonies in a federal courtroom in Wilmington, Delaware. And it was breaking my heart,” he wrote.
Former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre made a similar claim in her memoir released last year, arguing that the Delaware trial “had to be straining Biden’s spirit.”
“And frankly, I think his heart broke,” Jean-Pierre said of Hunter’s conviction.
Biden, 83, argued that the case against his only living son was politically motivated, despite being prosecuted by his own Department of Justice.

“It was obvious. Hunter was being raked over the coals because of me,” the former president wrote. “I knew the Republicans were using Hunter to hurt me. But my bigger concern was that they were determined to keep piling on the pressure until they broke him.”
Biden said the prosecution “failed to break Hunter,” before adding, “But I would be lying if I didn’t admit that they took a piece out of me.”

The former president said the Atlanta debate — which took place 16 days after Hunter was found guilty of lying about his drug addiction on federal forms when he purchased a firearm — “didn’t feel right from the start.”

Elsewhere in the book, a 480-page account of Biden’s one term as president, the ex-commander-in-chief reveals that he once threatened to campaign against Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia for opposing the $1.9 trillion COVID-19 relief package, until the Democrat-turned-independent pointed out that may actually be politically advantageous to him.

“This was my first major legislative initiative. The American people needed relief. I needed him on this vote,” Biden wrote. “I never considered myself a Lyndon Johnson–type president, who cajoled and threatened and even physically cowed legislators, but I was losing my temper.
“I told Joe that I needed him on this, and if he screwed me, I’d go to every county in West Virginia and tell them that Joe Manchin was why they weren’t getting any help.”
Manchin responded by reminding Biden that the then-president “wasn’t so popular in West Virginia.”
The centrist senator eventually voted in favor of the legislation.
Biden also revealed the contents of a “gracious note” Trump left him upon leaving the White House in January 2021.
“In his trademark blocky script, in heavy Sharpie ink, [Trump] had addressed the envelope ‘To ‘46,’” Biden wrote.
In the letter, Trump described Biden as someone he believed “will be true to yourself and the American people.”

“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” Trump wrote. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”
Biden said the “warm language” language made it seem like the letter was “coming from an old friend.”

articles.headline: 6 Chrome settings tweaks every power user needs to know
keyFacts: ZDNet outlined six Chrome settings adjustments to help users improve security, enhance privacy, and minimize distractions.
The author stated that blocking third-party cookies and location tracking protects user anonymity and personal safety.
The guide also recommends disabling site notifications, turning off browser password saving, and customizing file download locations.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- If you want to get the most out of Chrome, consider these changes.
- You’ll get better security and privacy, fewer interruptions, and more done.
- All of these changes are simple to make.

Whether you’re a longtime Chrome user, or just now switching to Google’s browser, you might assume that Chrome is perfectly fine right out of the box. That’s understandable, given that Chrome is the most widely used browser on the planet.
Also: Chrome running slow? 5 easy ways to speed it up fast

But Chrome’s default experience could use some improvement (as is the case with most software). Where do you start? I’m going to address what I believe are the most important changes to make in Chrome, so I won’t talk about appearance, tabs, or speed. This is mostly about privacy, security, and minimizing general annoyances, so you can get the best experience with Google’s browser.
More from ZDNET
1. Enhanced or Standard Protection

The single most important thing you can do in any browser is to enable the best protection it offers for your needs. In Chrome, this all starts with Enhanced Protection. Note: Enhanced Protection is typically the default, but this setting is so important that you should check to ensure it’s enabled.
Chrome offers three different protection settings:

- Enhanced Protection: Warns about dangerous sites, runs in-depth scans for suspicious downloads, protects across Google services, improves general security, and sends URLs of sites you visit to Google Safe Browsing.
- Standard Protection: Protects against sites, downloads, and extensions.
- No Protection: does not protect you.
Also: I’ve used nearly every browser — these are my top 4

There is one thing to keep in mind about Enhanced Protection: you lose some privacy because more data is sent to Google. With Enhanced Protection enabled, you share what you download and view with Google. If privacy is as important to you as important security, you could drop down to Standard Protection, because it’s still going to protect you against most threats.
This setting is configured in Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Security.
2. Block third-party cookies

Third-party cookies are there to create profiles of you that can be used for marketing and targeting. Cookies track you and send information to third parties — information that you might not otherwise want them to have.

Blocking third-party cookies helps to prevent cross-site tracking, reduce targeted ads, protect your anonymity and privacy, avoid security vulnerabilities, and prevent fingerprinting. I always recommend that users disable third-party cookies in Chrome, even if it can cause some sites to not load properly. The reason: You simply can’t trust those third parties. Who are they, and who is handling the information saved in those cookies?
Also: How to turn on Google’s new scam protection
If disabling third-party cookies breaks certain sites in Chrome, open them in a different browser (that also has third-party cookies disabled). If that browser doesn’t work, try another.
That’s how strongly I feel about blocking third-party cookies.
To block third-party cookies in Chrome, go to Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Third-party cookies and make sure they are blocked.
3. Block location access

With location access enabled, you could find yourself in a situation where your privacy and safety are compromised. Why is this an issue? Well, location access tracks your physical whereabouts. Consider the following two scenarios:
- There’s a ne’er-do-well wanting to keep tabs on where you are. With enough information and skill, location access could help that person track you down.
- You’ve gone on vacation and are using Chrome with location access turned on. The wrong person could pinpoint your location, know that you’re out of town, and break into your house.

To avoid becoming a victim of such situations, all you have to do is block location access, which is done in Chrome > Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Permissions > Location. On that page, make sure “Don’t allow sites to see your location” is selected.
4. Disable password saving

Yes, this one’s an inconvenience, but a web browser’s built-in password manager is simply not as safe as a dedicated password manager like KeePassXC. A dedicated password manager does one thing, and does it well; it helps you manage your passwords in a protected, encrypted vault.

When you save passwords to your web browser, it is possible that a malicious site or script could access those passwords and wreak havoc on your life. When you use a dedicated password manager, that browser isn’t going to have direct access to your credentials, which is exponentially safer.
Also: The best password managers: Expert tested
To disable password saving, go to Chrome > Passwords and autofill > Google Password Manager > Settings and click the On/Off slider for “Offer to save passwords and passkeys.”
5. Disable notifications

If you’re like me, a constant barrage of notifications is not just annoying — it’s distracting. Every time a notification pops up, my attention is stolen from whatever it is that I’m doing, which means I have to spend extra time getting back into the groove. If that happens constantly, I struggle to get anything done.

To that end, I disable notifications in my web browsers, my desktops, and even on the lock screen of my Android phones. I then get to decide when I’m distracted (and it usually happens after I finish a task).
Also: 5 ways to improve your Chrome browser’s security
To disable notifications in Chrome, go to Settings > Privacy and security > Site settings > Notifications and check “Don’t allow sites to send notifications.”
6. Enable ‘Ask where to save downloads’

If you allow Chrome to dictate where downloads are saved, you could wind up with a directory full of random things. I like to be the conductor of those downloads and where they are saved for two reasons:
- It prevents a single directory from getting crammed full of unrelated items.
- It allows me to keep downloads organized.

For example, I download a lot of .deb and .AppImage files on Linux, and I certainly don’t want them all going into the Downloads directory. I also download a lot of documents and ISO images, neither of which should be saved to Downloads. If I left Chrome as is, all those files would be saved in Downloads, which would not only fill that directory but also make it harder for me to find what I’m looking for. Instead, I tell Chrome to ask me where to save every downloaded file.
To enable “Ask where to save downloads,” go to Settings > Downloads and make sure “Ask where to save each file before downloading” is enabled.

articles.headline: There Really Is No Escape From The Duolingo Owl, Who Will Soon Join Pokémon Go
keyFacts: Duolingo and Pokémon Go announced a crossover event unlocking bonuses and outfits for players starting November 17.
Completing Duolingo lessons will grant a Pokémon Go promo code for timed research and exclusive creature backgrounds.
Pokémon Go is also launching a feature to view creature names in multiple languages and a separate collaboration with Crocs.
body: Not content with plaguing your phone's lock screen, Duo the Duolingo owl is next set to appear in Pokémon Go .
A crossover between the two hugely-popular smartphone apps has been announced, unlocking bonuses for players in both experiences. (Sadly, no, you won't be able to trap Duo in a Pokéball forever.)

The fun begins on November 17, when a time-limited event begins in Duolingo that requires you to complete at least one language lesson on seven separate days. This will then unlock a series of Pokémon-themed outfits for your Duolingo profile.

Completing all of that will also grant a promo code for Pokémon Go, unlocking timed research that awards Pokémon such as Pikachu and regional exclusive Chatot with a unique Duolingo background. It's rather cute — even if it does feature more of Duo the owl, too.

Why is all of this happening? While Pokémon Go has featured sponsored cosmetic items in the past, the game rarely offers this level of collaboration, and particularly not with another smartphone app. Still, earlier this year, the game also partnered with LEGO to offer similar bonus gameplay, centered around LEGO stores.

More prescient, perhaps, is the rollout of a new feature within Pokémon Go that will allow players to view the name of their creatures in multiple languages for the first time. While Pikachu is known as Pikachu the world over, other species have some very different names on foreign shores. (Snorlax is "Relaxo" in German, for example.)

And finally, in other Pokémon Go collaboration news, the creature catching app will soon feature a crossover with Crocs, the shoe brand that already offers a range of Pokémon clogs. All players can now unlock a virtual pair of Pikachu shoes by entering the promo code "POKEMONGOxCROCSxELECTRIFYING". Owners of the real-life Gengar and Jigglypuff shoes, meanwhile, will get codes for similar virtual versions of their own footwear.

articles.headline: US extends chip sale restrictions to more Asian countries to reduce risk of ‘diversion’ to China
keyFacts: The US Commerce Department restricted advanced chip sales and banned remote GPU access in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
The US government stated the rules aim to prevent foreign actors from using American technology to threaten national security.
Analyst Neil Shah said affected datacenter operators must now verify customer workloads or risk losing access to US chips.
body: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has decided to ban remote access to certain GPUs and servers running in datacenters located in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

The agency has also introduced a requirement to secure a license before selling what it describes as “advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers” that are sufficiently powerful to “be used for training or running of advanced SI models” into the five nations.

The interim final rule [PDF] containing the new regulations says they’re needed “to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Similar language can be found in previous US bans on sales of GPUs and other advanced tech to China, which Washington fears will use advanced tech to improve its military capabilities.

US authorities understood that export bans wouldn’t prevent Chinese entities from renting GPUs housed elsewhere. So from 2021 to 2024, Washington introduced a series of regulations that required US-based clouds to make sure they didn’t serve Chinese customers.

No such obligation existed for cloud operators elsewhere, which created a market for resources that Chinese customers could access from afar. It is widely felt that datacenter building booms in Malaysia and Thailand, both of which are generally on good terms with China, aimed to cater to Middle Kingdom customers who wanted to rent GPUs they could not import.

Megapseed – whose former employee Alice Huang had an intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and may have been a Chinese intelligence asset – built datacenters in Malaysia and was suspected of catering largely to offshore customers.
Neil Shah, vice president of research at analyst firm Counterpoint, said the new rules shift the regulatory burden of complying with export controls from hardware manufacturers to cloud operators.

“Data center operators in hubs such as Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia will now face massive ‘Know Your Customer's Workload’ requirements,” he told The Register by email, likening it to the KYC restrictions imposed on financial services firms. “They must prove to US regulators that their compute is not being funneled back to embargoed nations, or risk losing their own access to US silicon.”
He feels the new rules represent “a severe short-term compute bottleneck for Chinese tech giants” and “a massive long-term catalyst for decoupling.”
“Washington is forcing domestic capital and engineering talent to double down on full-stack sovereign alternatives, accelerating ecosystems like Huawei's Ascend.”

Shah’s observation came days after Alibaba decided to spin out its T-Head chip design unit, which it described as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China.” That description suggests Alibaba doesn’t think T-Head has strong prospects of selling its wares outside China.

It remains to be seen if the new BIS rules will slow datacenter development across Asia and Brazil. All five nations the US has regulated are all enjoying the economic impact of the AI boom. They’re also trying to manage its impact. Singapore limits datacenter construction, as befits a tiny and resource-constrained island nation. Malaysia is very much open for business but has introduced increasingly strict building codes and requirements to minimize energy and water consumption. Thailand recently introduced new regulations that new builds of large datacenters must take place in designated industrial zones. Indonesia also has strong regulations but is not currently a major datacenter hub.
Brazil requires datacenter operators to reserve at least 10 percent of capacity for local users, suggesting some operators are more interested in offshore customers.

Interestingly, the new BIS rules don’t impact infrastructure used for “commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat.”

Chinese e-tailers operate at vast scale and have already attracted regulatory attention in Europe and the USA. Asian and Brazilian datacenter operators therefore probably do not see the likes of Temu and Alibaba as a lifeline, but might see a role as regional hosts for outfits like Amazon or Meta. ®

articles.headline: School Campuses Emerge as the Latest Battleground for Flock Safety Cameras
keyFacts: Dozens of schools are reconsidering or discontinuing contracts with Flock Safety for license plate reader cameras amid student protests.
Attorney Amy Peikoff stated that storing location histories without suspicion enables abuse and violates the Fourth Amendment.
Flock stated its cameras help solve crimes and do not identify who is inside a vehicle.
body: Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.

Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.

A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties. Some of the schools that have walked away from Flock include Cornell University, Emory University, Penn State University and Stanford University, where a coalition called Safe Stanford successfully organized to convince school officials. At Stanford, the university chose to switch from Flock to technology from Genetec, which stores data for only an hour and doesn’t share information with third parties.
More from CNET

Some of the most recent campus protests against using Flock technology have been on the University of Iowa campus, where 2,000 petition signatures were delivered to campus police, and at the University of Kentucky, where student groups chanted, “Flock out! Flock off!”

Flock, which is one of several companies, including Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions and Palantir Technologies, that provide surveillance hardware and software to law enforcement, has been heavily criticized for license plate reader failure rates and abuses within law enforcement.

In an email to CNET, the Atlanta-based company declined to offer the number of colleges or schools it works with, though a recent research paper published in Policing & Society put the number at around 150.
Flock stressed in its email to CNET that customers it contracts with own and control their own data.

“Students deserve to feel safe at school, and Flock license plate reader technology has a measurable impact on helping to solve crimes and increase public safety,” the spokesperson said. “Flock LPR cameras capture a point-in-time image of the rear of a vehicle. Flock does not use facial recognition, cannot identify who is inside a vehicle and cannot determine who the vehicle is registered to.”
Implications for schools with surveillance

When government agencies like police departments or county sheriff’s offices employ a company like Flock to provide surveillance services, it typically involves installing cameras in public locations and pointing them at street intersections or on buildings.
College and high school campuses may have different rules for on-campus surveillance and for public schools. They might also be bound by state laws that also apply to government agencies.

“Campuses also raise issues ordinary public streets don’t: students often live there, many are minors, and student-privacy laws and school-search rules vary by state, as do limits on how long plate data can be kept and shared,” said Amy Peikoff, an attorney for the Pacific Legal Foundation.

Peikoff said that most courts have allowed the collection of the types of data Flock Safety collects. However, Peikoff said that problems can arise regarding how long agencies such as police departments or schools can retain the data they collect. In the past, activists have pointed to abuses that have occurred when law enforcement workers inappropriately accessed or shared information collected by Flock, in some cases, using it for stalking.

“Maintaining a vast, queryable database of location histories of individuals about whom there’s no particularized suspicion not only presents an opportunity for abuse, but is in itself, I believe, a Fourth Amendment violation,” Peikoff said.
